stem: A website password is made of three different capital letters followed by two digits. The digits may be the same. For example, KQB07 and ABC55 are allowed, but AAB12 is not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of possible passwords.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of possible passwords in which the three letters are in alphabetical order.

idea: Multiply the number of choices for each position. When the order of the letters is fixed (alphabetical), only the choice of the three letters matters, so use combinations.

solution.label: b
steps: Each set of three different letters can be written in alphabetical order in exactly one way, so count the sets: \(\dbinom{26}{3} = 2600\).
\(2600 \times 100\). (Check: the \(3! = 6\) orders of each set are now counted once, and \(1\,560\,000 \div 6 = 260\,000\).)

stem: Consider the different arrangements of the seven letters of the word BANANAS.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of these arrangements in which the two letters N are not next to each other.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of these arrangements that begin and end with the letter A.

idea: With repeated letters, divide \(n!\) by the factorial of each repeat count. For “not next to each other”, count the arrangements where they are together and subtract.

solution.label: a
steps: There are 7 letters with A three times and N twice: \(\dfrac{7!}{3!\,2!} = \dfrac{5040}{12}\).

solution.label: b
steps: Glue the two N's into one block. Then there are 6 items (B, A, A, A, NN, S), with A three times: \(\dfrac{6!}{3!} = 120\) arrangements have the N's together.

solution.label: c
steps: Fix an A at each end. The five middle letters are B, A, N, N, S, with N twice: \(\dfrac{5!}{2!}\).

stem: A club of 9 people chooses a committee of four: a chair, a secretary and two ordinary members. One person cannot hold two places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different committees that can be chosen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two of the club members, Ali and Bea, refuse to serve on the committee together. Find the number of committees that can now be chosen.

idea: The chair and the secretary are different jobs, so their order matters. The two ordinary members are not distinguished, so they are a combination. For part (b), count the committees with both Ali and Bea and subtract.

solution.label: b
steps: Committees with both Ali and Bea:
Both are officers: 2 ways to give them the two jobs, and \(\dbinom{7}{2} = 21\) choices of members, so 42.
One officer and one member: 2 choices of who is the officer, 2 choices of which job, 7 choices for the other officer and 6 for the other member, so \(2 \times 2 \times 7 \times 6 = 168\).
Both are members: \(7 \times 6 = 42\) choices of chair and secretary.

stem: Four-digit numbers are made from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7. No digit may be used more than once in a number.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find how many such four-digit numbers can be made.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find how many of these numbers are greater than 5000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find how many of these numbers are greater than 5000 and even.

idea: Fill the positions with the most restrictions first. In part (c) the first digit and the last digit both have conditions, and they interact when the first digit is 6, so split into cases.

solution.label: b
steps: The first digit must be 5, 6 or 7: 3 choices. The other three positions: \(6 \times 5 \times 4\).

solution.label: c
steps: First digit 5 or 7 (odd): the last digit is 2, 4 or 6, so 3 choices; the middle two: \(5 \times 4 = 20\). This gives \(2 \times 3 \times 20 = 120\).
First digit 6: the last digit is 2 or 4, so 2 choices; the middle two: \(5 \times 4 = 20\). This gives 40.

stem: A diagonal of a polygon is a line segment joining two vertices that are not next to each other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that a convex polygon with \(n\) sides has \(\dfrac{n(n - 3)}{2}\) diagonals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A convex polygon has 35 diagonals. Find the number of sides.

parts.label: c
parts.text: For the polygon in part (b), find the number of triangles whose three vertices are vertices of the polygon and none of whose sides is a side of the polygon.

idea: Every pair of vertices gives either a side or a diagonal. In part (c), count all triangles and remove those that use one side or two sides of the polygon.

solution.label: a
steps: There are \(\dbinom{n}{2} = \dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2}\) pairs of vertices, and \(n\) of these pairs are sides.

solution.label: c
steps: Triangles using two sides: three consecutive vertices. There are 10 of these, one for each middle vertex.
Triangles using exactly one side: choose the side (10 ways), then a third vertex that is not next to either end of it: \(10 - 4 = 6\) ways. This gives 60.

subtopic: Extended binomial theorem and partial fractions

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express \(f(x)\) in partial fractions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find \(\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx\).

idea: Write \(f(x) = \dfrac{A}{x - 1} + \dfrac{B}{x + 2}\), multiply through by the denominator, and choose values of \(x\) that make one bracket zero.

solution.label: b
steps: Each term integrates to a logarithm. For \(x > 1\) both brackets are positive.

subtopic: Extended binomial theorem and partial fractions
stem: Consider the expansion of \((1 - 2x)^{-1/2}\) in ascending powers of \(x\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the first three terms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the values of \(x\) for which the expansion is valid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: By choosing a suitable value of \(x\), use your answer to part (a) to find an approximation for \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{0.96}}\).

idea: For any rational \(n\), \((1 + y)^n = 1 + ny + \dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2!}y^2 + \cdots\), valid for \(|y| < 1\). Here \(y = -2x\) and \(n = -\frac{1}{2}\).

solution.label: c
steps: \(1 - 2x = 0.96\) when \(x = 0.02\), which is inside the interval of validity.

subtopic: Extended binomial theorem and partial fractions

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express \(f(x)\) in partial fractions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the expansion of \(f(x)\) in ascending powers of \(x\), up to and including the term in \(x^3\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the values of \(x\) for which this expansion is valid.

idea: Split \(f\) into two simple fractions, expand each as a geometric series, and add. The whole expansion is valid only where both parts are valid.

solution.label: b
steps: Add the two series term by term.

solution.label: c
steps: The first series needs \(|x| < 1\) and the second needs \(|2x| < 1\). Both hold when \(|x| < \frac{1}{2}\).

subtopic: Extended binomial theorem and partial fractions
stem: The expansion of \((1 + ax)^n\) in ascending powers of \(x\) begins \(1 - 6x + 27x^2\), where \(n\) is a negative integer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(na = -6\) and \(n(n - 1)a^2 = 54\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of \(n\) and the value of \(a\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the coefficient of \(x^3\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the values of \(x\) for which the expansion is valid.

idea: Compare coefficients with \(1 + nax + \dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2}a^2x^2 + \cdots\). Squaring the first equation lets you remove \(a\).

solution.label: a
steps: The coefficient of \(x\) is \(na = -6\). The coefficient of \(x^2\) is \(\dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2}a^2 = 27\), so \(n(n - 1)a^2 = 54\).

solution.label: b
steps: Square the first equation: \(n^2a^2 = 36\). Divide the second by this: \(\dfrac{n(n - 1)}{n^2} = \dfrac{54}{36}\), so \(\dfrac{n - 1}{n} = \dfrac{3}{2}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(zw\) in the form \(a + bi\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find \(\dfrac{z}{w}\) in the form \(a + bi\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down \(\left|\dfrac{z}{w}\right|\).

idea: Multiply out brackets using \(i^2 = -1\). To divide, multiply the top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator, which makes the denominator real.

stem: Let \(z = -\sqrt{3} + i\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the modulus and the argument of \(z\), and write \(z\) in the form \(re^{i\theta}\), where \(-\pi < \theta \le \pi\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find \(z^2\) in the form \(a + bi\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find \(z^6\).

idea: In exponential form, powers are easy: \(\left(re^{i\theta}\right)^n = r^n e^{in\theta}\). Draw \(z\) on an Argand diagram to place its argument in the right quadrant.

solution.label: a
steps: \(|z| = \sqrt{3 + 1} = 2\). The point \((-\sqrt{3}, 1)\) is in the second quadrant, at angle \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) above the negative real axis, so \(\arg z = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\).

stem: This question is about the equation \(z^2 = -5 + 12i\), where \(z \in \mathbb{C}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: By writing \(z = a + bi\), where \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\), find the two solutions of \(z^2 = -5 + 12i\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence solve the equation \(w^2 + 2w + 6 - 12i = 0\).

idea: Expand \((a + bi)^2\) and compare real and imaginary parts. In part (b) the quadratic formula needs the square root of a complex number, which part (a) supplies.

stem: The equation \(z^3 + az^2 + bz + 5 = 0\), where \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\), has a root \(z = 2 - i\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down a second root of the equation. Give a reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the third root, and the values of \(a\) and \(b\).

idea: A polynomial with real coefficients has its non-real roots in conjugate pairs. The product of the two conjugate roots gives a real quadratic factor.

solution.label: a
steps: The coefficients are real, so the conjugate of a root is also a root.

solution.label: b
steps: So \(z^3 + az^2 + bz + 5 = (z^2 - 4z + 5)(z + c)\). The constant terms give \(5c = 5\), so \(c = 1\) and the third root is \(-1\).

stem: On an Argand diagram, the point P represents \(z = 3 + i\). The point Q represents the complex number obtained when P is rotated anticlockwise about the origin O through \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) and then enlarged from O by scale factor 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the complex number represented by Q in the form \(a + bi\), giving exact values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact area of triangle OPQ.

idea: Multiplying by \(re^{i\theta}\) rotates a point about the origin through \(\theta\) and scales its distance from the origin by \(r\).

stem: Let \(z = e^{i\theta}\), where \(-\pi < \theta < \pi\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(\dfrac{z - 1}{z + 1} = i\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find, in the form \(a + bi\), the complex number \(z\) with \(|z| = 1\) for which \(\dfrac{z - 1}{z + 1} = \sqrt{3}\,i\).

idea: Take out the factor \(e^{i\theta/2}\) from the top and the bottom. What is left is \(e^{i\theta/2} \mp e^{-i\theta/2}\), and these are \(2i\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\) and \(2\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\).

solution.label: a
steps: \(e^{i\theta/2} - e^{-i\theta/2} = 2i\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2}\) and \(e^{i\theta/2} + e^{-i\theta/2} = 2\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2}\), which is not zero because \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < \dfrac{\theta}{2} < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

solution.label: b
steps: Check: \(\dfrac{z - 1}{z + 1} = \dfrac{-\frac{3}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i}{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i}\); multiplying top and bottom by \(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i\) makes the denominator \(\frac{1}{4} + \frac{3}{4} = 1\) and the numerator \(-\frac{3}{4} + \frac{3}{4} + \sqrt{3}\,i = \sqrt{3}\,i\).

stem: Consider the equation \(z^2 = 2i\,z^*\), where \(z \in \mathbb{C}\) and \(z^*\) is the complex conjugate of \(z\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: By writing \(z = x + iy\), where \(x, y \in \mathbb{R}\), show that \(x^2 - y^2 = 2y\) and \(xy = x\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find all the solutions of the equation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the non-zero solutions are the vertices of an equilateral triangle with its centre at the origin.

idea: Compare real parts and imaginary parts. The equation \(xy = x\) splits into two cases, \(x = 0\) or \(y = 1\); treat each case separately.

solution.label: a
steps: Real parts: \(x^2 - y^2 = 2y\). Imaginary parts: \(2xy = 2x\), so \(xy = x\).

solution.label: b
steps: If \(y = 1\): \(x^2 - 1 = 2\), so \(x = \pm\sqrt{3}\). This gives \(z = \sqrt{3} + i\) and \(z = -\sqrt{3} + i\).

solution.label: c
steps: \(|\sqrt{3} + i| = |-\sqrt{3} + i| = |-2i| = 2\), so all three lie on the circle of radius 2 about the origin.

Their arguments are \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\), \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\) and \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\), which differ by \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\) each time. Three points equally spaced round a circle form an equilateral triangle centred at the centre of the circle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write \(z\) in the form \(r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find \(z^{10}\) in the form \(a + bi\).

idea: De Moivre's theorem: \(\left[r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\right]^n = r^n(\cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta)\). Raise the modulus to the power and multiply the argument.

solution.label: b
steps: \(\dfrac{5\pi}{2}\) is the same angle as \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so this is \(32(0 + i)\).

stem: Consider the equation \(z^4 = -16\), where \(z \in \mathbb{C}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the four roots of the equation, giving your answers in the form \(a + bi\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence write \(z^4 + 16\) as the product of two quadratic factors with real coefficients.

idea: Write \(-16\) in modulus-argument form, allowing for adding multiples of \(2\pi\) to the argument, then take the fourth root. Pairs of conjugate roots give real quadratic factors.

solution.label: b
steps: Pair each root with its conjugate. For \(\sqrt{2} \pm \sqrt{2}\,i\): sum \(2\sqrt{2}\), product \(2 + 2 = 4\), giving \(z^2 - 2\sqrt{2}\,z + 4\).

stem: Let \(u = \sqrt{3} + i\) and \(v = 1 - i\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write \(u\) and \(v\) in the form \(re^{i\theta}\), where \(-\pi < \theta \le \pi\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find \(\dfrac{u^7}{v^4}\) in the form \(a + bi\), giving exact values.

idea: In exponential form, powers multiply the argument and a quotient subtracts arguments. Convert back to Cartesian form only at the end.

stem: Let \(z = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use de Moivre's theorem to show that \(z^n + z^{-n} = 2\cos n\theta\), for \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: By expanding \(\left(z + z^{-1}\right)^4\), show that \(\cos^4\theta = \dfrac{1}{8}\left(\cos 4\theta + 4\cos 2\theta + 3\right)\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^4\theta\,d\theta\).

idea: \(z + z^{-1} = 2\cos\theta\), so \(\left(z + z^{-1}\right)^4 = 16\cos^4\theta\). Expanding the same expression with the binomial theorem and pairing \(z^k\) with \(z^{-k}\) turns powers into multiple angles.

solution.label: a
steps: \(z^n = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta\) and \(z^{-n} = \cos(-n\theta) + i\sin(-n\theta) = \cos n\theta - i\sin n\theta\).

solution.label: b
steps: By part (a) this is \(2\cos 4\theta + 8\cos 2\theta + 6\). Also \(\left(z + z^{-1}\right)^4 = (2\cos\theta)^4 = 16\cos^4\theta\).

stem: Consider the equation \(z^5 = 1\), where \(z \in \mathbb{C}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the five roots in the form \(e^{i\theta}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the sum of the five roots is zero.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence show that \(\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5} + \cos\dfrac{4\pi}{5} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Using \(\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{5} = 2\cos^2\dfrac{2\pi}{5} - 1\), show that \(\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{4}\).

idea: The roots form a geometric sequence with ratio \(\omega = e^{2\pi i/5}\), so their sum is a geometric series. The real part of a sum is the sum of the real parts, and the roots come in conjugate pairs.

solution.label: b
steps: With \(\omega = e^{2\pi i/5}\), the sum is \(1 + \omega + \omega^2 + \omega^3 + \omega^4 = \dfrac{\omega^5 - 1}{\omega - 1}\), a geometric series with \(\omega \ne 1\).

solution.label: c
steps: \(e^{8\pi i/5}\) is the conjugate of \(e^{2\pi i/5}\), and \(e^{6\pi i/5}\) is the conjugate of \(e^{4\pi i/5}\), so their real parts are equal.
Real part of the sum: \(1 + 2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5} + 2\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{5} = 0\). Subtract 1 and divide by 2.

solution.label: d
steps: \(0 < \dfrac{2\pi}{5} < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so \(c > 0\), and we take the positive root.

stem: Each statement below is false. Disprove each one with a counterexample.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For every positive integer \(n\), the number \(n^2 + n + 41\) is prime.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For every real number \(x\), \(x^2 \ge x\).

idea: One example where the statement fails is enough to disprove a claim about every case. Show the calculation that makes it fail.

solution.label: b
steps: Try a number between 0 and 1, for example \(x = \dfrac{1}{2}\): \(x^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}\), which is less than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).

stem: You may assume that \(\sqrt{6}\) is irrational.
Prove, by contradiction, that \(\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3}\) is irrational.
idea: Assume the opposite: that \(\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3}\) equals a rational number \(r\). Squaring produces \(\sqrt{6}\) on its own, written in terms of \(r\).

steps: Assume that \(\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3} = r\), where \(r\) is rational.
\(r^2 - 5\) is rational, and half of a rational number is rational, so \(\sqrt{6}\) would be rational.
This contradicts the fact that \(\sqrt{6}\) is irrational. So the assumption is false.

stem: Use mathematical induction to prove that \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n} r \times r! = (n + 1)! - 1\), for all \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\).
idea: In the inductive step, add the next term \((k + 1)(k + 1)!\) to \((k + 1)! - 1\), then take out the common factor \((k + 1)!\).

steps: Let \(P(n)\) be the statement \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n} r \times r! = (n + 1)! - 1\).
\(n = 1\): the left side is \(1 \times 1! = 1\) and the right side is \(2! - 1 = 1\). So \(P(1)\) is true.
Assume \(P(k)\) is true for some \(k \in \mathbb{Z}^+\): \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{k} r \times r! = (k + 1)! - 1\).
\(P(1)\) is true, and \(P(k)\) true implies \(P(k + 1)\) true. So, by mathematical induction, \(P(n)\) is true for all \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\).

stem: Consider the product \(\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2^2}\right)\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{3^2}\right)\cdots\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{(n + 1)^2}\right)\), for \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove by mathematical induction that the product is equal to \(\dfrac{n + 2}{2(n + 1)}\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the value that the product approaches as \(n\) becomes large.

idea: In the inductive step, multiply the assumed result by the next factor, \(1 - \dfrac{1}{(k + 2)^2} = \dfrac{(k + 1)(k + 3)}{(k + 2)^2}\), and cancel.

solution.label: a
steps: Let \(P(n)\) be the statement that the product of the first \(n\) factors is \(\dfrac{n + 2}{2(n + 1)}\).
\(n = 1\): the product is \(1 - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4}\), and \(\dfrac{1 + 2}{2(1 + 1)} = \dfrac{3}{4}\). So \(P(1)\) is true.
Assume \(P(k)\) is true for some \(k \in \mathbb{Z}^+\). The product of the first \(k + 1\) factors is
\(P(1)\) is true, and \(P(k)\) true implies \(P(k + 1)\) true. So, by mathematical induction, \(P(n)\) is true for all \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\).

stem: This question is about the inequality \(n! > 2^n\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove by mathematical induction that \(n! > 2^n\) for all integers \(n \ge 4\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence show that \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=4}^{n} \frac{1}{r!} < \frac{1}{8}\) for all integers \(n \ge 4\).

idea: The base case is \(n = 4\), not \(n = 1\). For part (b), part (a) gives \(\dfrac{1}{r!} < \dfrac{1}{2^r}\), and the powers of \(\frac{1}{2}\) form a geometric series with a known sum to infinity.

solution.label: a
steps: \(n = 4\): \(4! = 24\) and \(2^4 = 16\), and \(24 > 16\). So the statement is true for \(n = 4\).
The statement is true for \(n = 4\), and true for \(n = k\) implies true for \(n = k + 1\). So, by mathematical induction, it is true for all integers \(n \ge 4\).

stem: This question is about irrational numbers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove by contradiction that \(\log_2 3\) is irrational.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence prove that \(\log_4 9\) is irrational.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give a counterexample to show that the sum of two irrational numbers is not always irrational.

idea: If \(\log_2 3 = \dfrac{p}{q}\), then \(2^p = 3^q\). One side is even and the other is odd.

solution.label: a
steps: Assume that \(\log_2 3 = \dfrac{p}{q}\), where \(p, q\) are integers and \(q > 0\). Since \(\log_2 3 > 0\), also \(p > 0\).
\(2^p\) is even (as \(p \ge 1\)), but \(3^q\) is odd, because a product of odd numbers is odd. An even number cannot equal an odd number.
This is a contradiction, so the assumption is false.

solution.label: c
steps: \(\sqrt{2}\) and \(-\sqrt{2}\) are both irrational, but their sum is 0, which is rational.

stem: A café sells coffee, tea and juice, each at a fixed price. Three orders were:
Order 1: two coffees, one tea and one juice, costing $12.
Order 2: one coffee, three teas and two juices, costing $17.
Order 3: three coffees, two teas and one juice, costing $17.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down a system of three equations for the prices \(c\), \(t\) and \(j\), in dollars, of a coffee, a tea and a juice.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve the system to find the price of each drink.

idea: Use one equation to remove the same unknown from the other two. That leaves two equations in two unknowns.

solution.label: b
steps: Second minus twice the first: \(c + 3t + 2j - (4c + 2t + 2j) = 17 - 24\), so \(-3c + t = -7\).

stem: The curve \(y = ax^2 + bx + c\) passes through the points \((1, 4)\), \((-1, 10)\) and \((2, 7)\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down three equations in \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the values of \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the least value of \(y\).

idea: Each point on the curve gives one linear equation in the three unknowns. Subtracting the first two removes \(a\) and \(c\) at once.

solution.label: a
steps: Substitute each point into \(y = ax^2 + bx + c\).

solution.label: b
steps: First minus second: \(2b = -6\), so \(b = -3\). Then \(a + c = 7\) and \(4a + c = 13\).

stem: Consider the system of equations
\[\begin{aligned} x + y + kz &= 1 \\ x + ky + z &= 1 \\ kx + y + z &= 1 \end{aligned}\]
where \(k \in \mathbb{R}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: By adding the three equations, show that \((k + 2)(x + y + z) = 3\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: For \(k \ne 1\) and \(k \ne -2\), show that the system has the unique solution \(x = y = z = \dfrac{1}{k + 2}\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the system has no solution when \(k = -2\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the solutions when \(k = 1\), and interpret them geometrically.

idea: The system is symmetric. Subtracting two equations gives a factor \((1 - k)\), which forces two of the unknowns to be equal unless \(k = 1\).

solution.label: b
steps: First minus second: \((1 - k)y + (k - 1)z = 0\), so \((1 - k)(y - z) = 0\). As \(k \ne 1\), \(y = z\).
Second minus third: \((1 - k)x + (k - 1)y = 0\), so \(x = y\) in the same way.
Then \(x = y = z\), and part (a) gives \(3(k + 2)x = 3\). As \(k \ne -2\), \(x = \dfrac{1}{k + 2}\). These steps leave no choice, so the solution is unique.

solution.label: c
steps: With \(k = -2\), part (a) says \(0 \times (x + y + z) = 3\), that is \(0 = 3\), which is impossible.
solution.answer: Adding the equations gives \(0 = 3\), a contradiction, so there is no solution.

solution.label: d
steps: With \(k = 1\) all three equations are \(x + y + z = 1\).
solution.answer: Infinitely many solutions: every point with \(x + y + z = 1\). The three planes are the same plane.
